utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please, and good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Case Number IT-03-68-T, the Prosecutor versus Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Mr. Oric, good morning to you. Can you follow the proceedings in your own language?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I can follow the proceedings in my own language.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down. Appearances for Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. My name is Jan Wubben, lead counsel for the Prosecution; also good morning to my learned friends of the Defence. I'm here together with co-counsel, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio, and Ms. Joanne Richardson, as well as our case manager, Ms. Donnica Henry-Frijlink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you and good morning to you and your team. Appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. I am Vasvija Vidovic, appearing for Mr. Oric, together with Mr. John Jones. Together with us are our legal assistant, Ms. Adisa Mehic, and our case manager, Mr. Geoff Roberts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, and good morning to you and your team. So any preliminaries before we bring in the witness?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, two brief issues. During the Prosecutor's case in our cross-examination, we were very fair. Yesterday I looked at the information as to how and when we submitted our lists of exhibits to be used during the cross-examination, and I established that in a large number of cases those lists were submitted as soon as we received the proofing notes, in other words before the witnesses came to testify. Those that we did not submit in that way were submitted within the due time for the Prosecutors to get ready. Yesterday I spoke to Ms. Richardson. I asked her when we would receive the proofing notes and she said this would be around 4.00 or 5.00. We expected those. I waited. The time went by. It was already 9.00. I called all the telephone numbers that were available to me, including the case manager. I left a number of messages, and finally around 9.00 in the afternoon, I believe that it was 5 minutes after 9.00, I called the security and I kindly asked them to check whether there was anybody in the Office of the Prosecutor. Mr. Ray from the security checked and told me there was nobody there. He was very kind. He did his best to help me. And then I asked him to make a note of that. At 10.15, I received a list finally. This list had been sent, I suppose, from somebody from the OTP. That person probably sent it from home. And what raised my biggest concern and what made me even cross was the fact that it says on the list that the Prosecutor would be using three tapes from P329, from the interview of our Prosecutor. This is a very voluminous material which I tried to study, but I didn't have time. Today when I came here at quarter past 8.00 it says here that the Prosecutor will be using P328 and the tape from that exhibit, which does not allow me any possibility to look into that document to see what it is about. I think this is not fair. This is not how we behaved. It is the Prosecutor's duty to be fair not to us as their colleagues, but to the accused. The accused has to be in the position to get the information to help us represent him. I would kindly ask you to order the Prosecutor to behave in the way that will enable us to prepare ourselves or the cross-examination. If not, if things continue in this way, then we will decide not to be fair in turn. We used to deliver our lists for cross-examination a day before we actually started our cross-examination. That is the first issue, Your Honours. And the second issue is also brief. It is very difficult for me to believe that what I agree with the Prosecutor will be honoured, and since we are short of time, just for the record, I would like to say the following. There was a correspondence between the Prosecutor and ourselves about some very important materials that have to do with the Defence case. I'm talking about the materials of the -- from the archives of the Drina Corps that the Prosecutor's office seized from the Government of Republika Srpska some half a year ago. This is the public archives of Bosnia and Herzegovina which is not in the possession of a source that we might be able to consult; it is in their hands. We were corresponding with them for two or three months. We never received a single document. Finally Mr. Wubben stood up in the courtroom and promised that these would be submitted to us before the beginning of July. Nothing happened. Mr. Di Fazio was fair. He explained and he said that he would do his utmost to help us and that these -- this is underway. Kindly appreciate that we need this material now. We have been given a deadline of two months. In order for me to be able to use this material, I have to have it before the next recess. If I receive an exculpatory material after that, the Prosecutor has to be aware of the position I will be in. Through my channels I have been able to obtain only two documents from that collection, and believe me they are absolutely exculpatory for my client. They refer to the attacks which are the subject of the indictment. These are my concerns at the moment and that's why I wanted both of these concerns to be on the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, and I think they are very valid concerns that, however, need to be responded to by the Prosecution before we address them. In the meantime, I would like the usher, please, to go to the witness and explain to him that there might be a slight delay and offer our apologies to him. Explain to him that we are discussing things that have got nothing to do with him. Ms. Trevisan, did you hear me? Yes, I don't know -- let's take them one by one. I would prefer to start with this last one which is the one which is more serious than the two -- of the two.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This last one, the Drina Corps documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I requested Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio to respond to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. I wish we'd been informed that this was going to be raised this morning, because then I might have been given an opportunity to spend ten minutes, that's all I would have needed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can spend ten minutes after the break, if you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If you need more details, after I finish my submission, I'll do that and I can come back to you later, but I can lay out our position pretty quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: There has been extensive correspondence about this matter toing and froing between the Defence and the Prosecution. Once again I repeat the submission that I have made in the past when these disclosure issues have come up and that's there's absolutely no reason for us to delay getting this material to them, absolutely none whatsoever and we have been doing what we can to get as much material to them about the Drina Corps as we can. The problem lies in researching the material. The Defence sent us some correspondence and the sequence of correspondence is important because there's a large -- a significant period of time when we sought further information. I think off the top of my head it was the first name of commanders -- they gave us surnames, but we needed the first names and there was a long time of getting that information from the Defence and eventually they got it. And as soon as they got it, searches were underway. And furthermore a significant proportion of that material has been available already on EDS. Some of the names they gave us were Mr. Deronjic, someone called Sic and Jisic and apparently they are already on EDS. So the matter has by no means - by no means - been left alone. On the contrary it's been attended to as fast as we could, as we could deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's presenting it in a very simple, placid manner, which with our experience on the Bench, we know immediately that there's still a lot of work to be done. What is of my -- of concern to us is that we have started the Defence case without this material being available in its entirety, as requested, and it seems, as promised -- as promised. What is of more concern is the Rule 68 material that may be contained in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, I appreciate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So because -- as far as Rule 68 material is concerned, it's no excuse coming forward and saying this is in the -- in the electronic data system and it is therefore available.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It doesn't work like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: The problem is, if Your Honours please, purely and simply a question of research. If you want I can address you after the break and give you the full details. It sounds to me like it probably would be a better idea because the Prosecution is not going to accept what the Defence has said about this. The Prosecution has done whatever it can to accommodate within -- within its physical abilities to accommodate this and to deal with this. And we're trying, we're endeavouring to do this. The problem has been always refining the search parameters so the searches become more manageable and we get more targeted material and then getting it to the Defence whether by way of EDS or delivering large volumes of paper. But I can give you -- I'll go back and I'll - if you permit me - I'll go back during the break and I'll look at the correspondence and I'll come to you with the correspondence and I'll tell you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When did this -- I thank you, Mr. Di Fazio. When did this story start, the exchange of correspondence on these archives?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: January of this year?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in January, what have you received? Leave the EDS alone for the time being because EDS, you have the facility to access it, I would imagine, and if you haven't accessed it it's a case of mea culpa, but with regard to proper disclosure what has been going on?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, in our first letter we provided plenty criteria so that a number of documents could be found. We did not provide the names of the commanders of the brigades that we didn't know at the moment. Then there were two letters in May, and in those letters on the -- on the 3rd of May we provided the full names of commanders and all the other criteria and it was promised at that moment that this would happen until June. If this existed on the EDS, I would not even ask for that. I claim that the correspondence that we are looking for cannot be found on the EDS. The documents of the Drina Corps have not been put on the EDS. There are some documents arising from those documents -- the commanders, but are of a different nature. We want reports of the Serbian units that participated in those attacks. The reports that they sent. These are the reports that we want because they're absolutely relevant and this is what we asked for on the 3rd of May. Not a single document have we received so far. Sometimes the criteria may have been too broad, but that doesn't mean that some of them could not have been met and some of the documents could not have been provided. I'm asking for this especially because in keeping with Rule 65(B) we asked for inspection. I asked for inspection and I said if you don't have resources and that is a problem, allow me to carry out an inspection of that archive in your presence. I will spend my time, my resources, and I will try and find what I need. This was not allowed to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, you will come back to us, Mr. Di Fazio, after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I will, I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And I suggest that you better be ready with an answer that clears the way for us to continue with the case because, if not, we will stop the case. And then we will suspend the proceedings until we are ensured that the Defence is provided with all the documentation that enables them to defend their client well. SO you better come --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I will come back to you, chapter and verse, with the correspondence of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not the correspondence; it's actually -- if these documents have been asked for as way back as January, I do accept, of course, that if you did not have clear parameters, certain researches had to wait. But I take it that you now have all the parameters.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, that's what the correspondence will reveal. So it's important that I show that to you because it will -- that I lead you through it, because only then will you understand how the story developed and only then will you understand how the Prosecution has been endeavouring to provide this material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I don't know how voluminous this material is because obviously I haven't seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No, you don't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is, obviously, again, one thing on which you are not agreeing. You're saying that it is on the EDS and Madam Vidovic is saying that none of it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Now, the picture is not that simple, with respect, Your Honour. There's -- some of it is on EDS. Now, I can find that out and I can give you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but at least the Defence should be told, "Listen, all of these documents from the Drina Corps archives are on EDS." And then she can -- he or her staff can look into it. Still, presence of these documents in EDS does not satisfy the Rule 68 disclosure, if you are aware that there is such exculpatory material. So at the end of the day, I don't want to allow the case to go forward and come -- find ourselves in a situation, either too late in the day or after that judgement has been handed down, that there was exculpatory material in this archive which was never disclosed and then blow the whole -- blow the whole case up. That is, if we come to a judgement which is contrary to -- against the accused because obviously that -- we don't know. But please, I hope I've made --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have got responsibilities that go much beyond the ones of disclosure that you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the other issue, the handing to the Defence of the list of -- do you want to address also this part about --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, before I give the floor to Ms. Joanne Richardson --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: To give the particular details of yesterday, I would like to underline that already in the 65 ter Conference we raised the issue of the vagueness of the summary -- of some of the summaries, and throughout the list of summaries we identified that those summaries of witnesses provided by the Defence are sometimes so general that it is hard to prepare oneself and that there is a need for further details. So today we will do a submission for some guideline. And in that respect, Mr. Gramsci Di Fazio will address the Court. But please be informed that we already were aware on Thursday and addressed the Senior Legal Officer to -- in that respect. And that gives a lot of difficulties for the Office of the Prosecutor to prepare on a solid base for any witnesses to come. This has to do -- also is one of the reasons why it is also difficult for my colleague, Ms. Joanne Richardson, to prepare solid for the witness we will -- who will testify today. I'll give the floor to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to the Defence. Your Honour, I'd first like to say that it was drawn to my attention yesterday by Madam Vidovic, who was very concerned about when the Prosecution would give the Defence a witness -- exhibit list, excuse me. I advised Madam Vidovic that in fact I would try my best to get it to her by 6.00. I did not say 4.00. And in fact, when the court session ended, I immediately returned to my office and started preparing the exhibit list. I just have to say that in respect to the summary that was provided, I'm glad that this was raised this morning, because, in fact, Your Honours, we look at the summaries that are very vague, very broad -- excuse me, the witness summaries, the Defence witness summaries. It really does hamper the Prosecution from providing an exhibit list in an efficient manner, in an early manner, to the Defence. We have a summary, for instance, with respect to this witness that's very vague where he's -- supposedly was supposed to testify about matters in the Vlasenica area. And indeed this witness has talked about, yesterday, matters involving Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Srebrenica, especially about speaking to Ferat Hodzic and other matters that were not in the summaries. So it was difficult to prepare beforehand and anticipate an exhibit list. So I should -- I should say that because the Defence is providing these very broad, vague summaries, it's really hampering us from in the future providing them with an exhibit list as early as they would like. Now, with respect to the timing, I myself left the office last night at 12.30. At 9.00 I received a call from security advising that a Madam Vidovic had called. He was very -- he said that she was unclear about what she wanted but she had been trying to reach me. Security had not been able to provide her with my extension. For some reason it's not -- they didn't have it available. So they contacted me about this phone call. I asked whether or not Ms. Vidovic had in fact left a phone number; they said she had not. I knew very well that she was calling about the exhibit list and I had been working feverishly to prepare for her. The case manager had already went home. I completed the exhibit list a little after 9.00 and we went it out immediately. The only thing I can say with respect to the tapes is that we do apologise for not being very specific with respect to the tapes that we were using. We will use them towards the end of the morning. But in fact, Your Honour, it was no intention deliberately on the part of the Prosecution to in any way hamper the Defence. I can only say that consideration needs to be given to the Prosecution with respect to these summaries which will indeed not only affect our preparation for cross-examination but will affect the exhibit list. And I should say with respect to what Madam Vidovic said about their providing the Prosecution with the exhibit list, in fact, is not entirely true. Indeed, during the Prosecution case we received exhibit lists late into the evening and sometimes the very morning of the cross-examination. So I do think that the Prosecution needs to be treated fairly and the Prosecution will make all reasonable efforts to get an exhibit list to the Defence as soon as it is reasonably possible to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is not yet enough electricity in the air, so I give you back the floor, Madam Vidovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all, I really can't understand this attitude. If I say that we received the submission at quarter past 10.00, then it wasn't at 9.00. And what Ms. Richardson is saying is simply not true. We have very good records on the times when we sent our lists to the Prosecutor and when they sent our lists to us. However, we are talking about a different issue here and this issue is always present. I am just looking at the professional attitude of every of our learned friends. When it comes to Ms. Richardson, we have the hardest time. Either she sends us a huge list of documents that she never uses, which she has done a number of times, or she makes similar mistakes. At 10.15 yesterday, she told us that she would use P329 with three tapes. I had to spend hours reading the transcripts of those tapes. This morning it was no longer P329 but P328. I was clear, I believe, Your Honour. Whatever I'm saying here, you have to believe me that I am telling the truth. I apologise, I forgot a very important thing. It is true that the Prosecutor at the 65 ter meeting raised the issue of the alleged vagueness of our summaries. The legal assistant to the Chamber deemed that they were clear enough, that they were not vague. So much from me when it comes to the summaries. And the summary for this witness was also rather clear. We said very clearly that the witness was in a position to be politically active from Tuzla and have influence in the relevant area.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I could just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just to clarify, when I said that the exhibit list --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this will be the last -- this will be the end of submissions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Of course. When I said the exhibit list was sent out, I meant that I sent the exhibit list to the case manager who then gathered -- who put it in the correct format and forwarded it to the Defence. Now, as I stand here making this submission, there is an indication and, for the record, that last October when the case started that the Prosecution received an exhibit list from the Defence at 10.30 in the evening prior to the cross-examination. And I raise that not to say that this will be our practice, but we are doing the best we can under the circumstances. And with respect to what Madam Vidovic said about the witness -- the witness exhibits that I have been providing, I have simply responded to the complaint that providing too many exhibits and too many documents and I don't use them subsequently hampers the Defence. So what I did last evenings was spend an enormous amount of time to narrow down the documents that I would use so it would be -- so it would not hamper the Defence and would be convenient for them. It seems that is also a problem for them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's cut it down to the basic essentials. Let's start with the Drina Corps. The Drina Corps, we will wait until after the break. We will hear what you have to say, Mr. Di Fazio. We reserve our position. We are not allowing -- going to allow a situation to obtain, whereby, particularly after the recess, we start again this case without these documents having been delivered entirely. In the meantime, and this is the position -- of course, I am speaking for the time being without having had the benefit of consulting my two clients -- my two Judges, sorry. In the meantime, may I please make it clear that whatever can be disclosed should be disclosed. You shouldn't wait until you have the entire dossier and then disclose it in bulk. In the meantime -- this should be an ongoing, rolling process. So if -- I can't imagine that since January all these researches that have been taking place have produced nothing. Whatever they have produced, they should be in the hands of the Defence, making it clear that this is an ongoing process, it is not ready, part of it is disclosed under Rule 68, part of it is disclosed under Rule 66, and it should go on. But I simply hope to God that you will not put it in a position where we really have to say: This is crucial. Because these documents may have been crucial in the very beginning in the preparation by the Defence of the case. So please do understand that. We are at the very early stages. So if there has been damage -- prejudice, we are - still at the stage - where that can be remedied, but don't let it go any further because if you do, then you are creating big problems for the Trial Chamber which will have to stop until this process is concluded --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: If Your Honours please, I'm hoping that after I've addressed you after the break and after you've given me an opportunity to go and see -- to look and refer to the correspondence, that expressions like "don't let it go any further" will simply become redundant and you will see -- you will see -- you will understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm glad to hear the, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: -- the point I'm trying to make. The Prosecution has not left this address alone, it has not. It has addressed it. And that's why I was so surprised to hear out of the blue this morning these submissions. So -- but as I said, allow me the opportunity to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And I'll take you through chapter and verse the proceedings -- the correspondence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Jones [sic], certainly, Mr. Jones. And my attention is being drawn by because -- yes, Mr. Di Fazio. My attention is being drawn by Judge Brydensholt to 66(B), particularly in light of what Ms. Vidovic has openly stated here, that she formally asked you to allow her to inspect these archives under your supervision, when I say "your," someone from your office. And this request, it seems, was not entertained. I do draw your attention to Rule 66(B), which lays down that the Prosecutor -- this may change a little bit in a short while, but for the time being this is how it is. "Prosecutor shall on request permit the Defence to inspect any books, documents, photographs, and tangible objects in the Prosecutor's custody or control which are material to the preparation of the Defence or are intended for use by the Prosecutor as evidence at trial or were obtained from or belonged to the accused." So we have these three possibilities. So please do keep that in mind as well. Thanks, Judge Brydensholt. The other matter, the other matter. The other matter, this is where trial experience from Bench and parties becomes very important. Such incidents are unavoidable. They happen in each and every case. I must also confess that this compared to other cases that I have been involved with, the summaries that have been provided by the Defence could definitely contain more detail, but they are certainly much less vague than summaries I have seen in other cases. So they do contain much more detail than summaries that I have had the opportunity to see in other cases. Still, of course, I do concede that there are certain areas which remain vague as you read them. The situation is also bound to change now as the Defence selects the 30 witnesses that they're -- maximum of 30 witnesses that they will be bringing forward, which possibly and probably would entail eliminating areas which we said we don't want to hear evidence about, and including in those summaries areas which previously those would have been dealt with by other witnesses and which now will be incorporated in the testimony of this maximum period -- maximum number of 30 witnesses. I do appreciate, because this happens in every case, that there is a slight difference between the position of the Defence and the position of the Prosecution in this context because usually during the Prosecution case you have statements which most of the time you don't have during the Defence -- the Defence case because the Defence usually does not come up with written statements or take statements of persons they have interviewed and who are testifying here. And that does place the Prosecution in a different position. Still, however, there is this overriding principle in trials. If you reduce the trial into a duel amongst yourself and everyone wants to draw the last drop of blood, then it will be -- you will be creating a tragic situation. You have the same responsibility that we have, to do your utmost in this search to find out the truth, a truth which would ultimately end up with the acquittal of the accused, or the truth which could ultimately send the accused to a long period of imprisonment. So they have got responsibility as Defence counsel, you have got responsibility as Prosecutors. With regard to cooperating during the trial itself in the production and -- of evidence and the concluding of the evidentiary state, you have to cooperate; if you don't cooperate, we will have to impose. We don't like to impose deadlines when it comes to when you should file the list of -- exhibit list, the exhibit list. I mean, you realise that we have had these incidents come and go during the trial and they were always sorted out whenever there was good faith. And I must say that there was always good faith. There were instances where rightfully Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic stood up and said, We have only received this. We have just been informed this morning that this document or this exhibit or the other exhibit are going to be made use of, or these exhibits are being tendered today for the first time; we haven't had an opportunity to see them. There were even requests for postponements, adjournments, et cetera, and then good faith always prevailed. Because I am sure that there is no one in this courtroom from your side or from that side that is relying on bad faith as a remedy or as a solution to the problems that may arise. It won't work and you would be very stupid, very foolish if you tried it. So may I suggest the following. I do realise, and I'm sure that the Defence realises also because they have passed through this, that it is not always easy at the end of the testimony of a client -- of a witness for -- brought forward by the other side to be in a position to draw up and forward to the opposite side, to the other party, a comprehensive exhibit list. However, I also believe because I have lived this as Defence counsel myself, that while you proceed during -- we had this witness testify for three hours yesterday or so. I'm sure that while you are proceeding you are identifying in your mind the documents that you will need to produce which will then be dug up with the help of the case manager. And any leftovers, I know that it's going to take you hours. But we are all working at a stressful rate here. And when you tell me, We're here until midnight, I quite believe you. But when Ms. Vidovic tells me that she was reading the transcript after half past 10.00 when she received notice that you were going to make use of tape 329 or whatever, I believe her, too. No one should be working at these rates and at this stressful -- I mean, I would prefer to see a much more comfortable and stress-free environment; unfortunately it's not like that. It's not like that for you and it's not like that for us. So when you bring up instances and incidents like these, we try to pacify the situation as much as we can. I don't think either party has been unreasonable -- willingly unreasonable in this case, in this area of exchanging information between you in preparation of either the examination-in-chief or cross-examination. This witness hasn't finished as yet. I don't know how long to expect him in the stand there, in the witness stand. What I expect from you throughout is that you try and finish this exercise at your earliest. If you see that it is going to present you with problems, then your duty is to get hold of Madam Vidovic, Mr. Jones, Mr. Roberts, or whoever, and say, I promised you my papers at 6.00. I'm sorry, I'm not in a position to provide them at 6.00, my list at 6.00. I will provide it at 9.00. And if at 9.00 you're not in a position to provide it, then you should ring up again -- when I say you, Ms. Richardson, today it's you, tomorrow it will be Mr. Di Fazio, the day after it will be Mr. Wubben, and the last day it will be Ms. Sellers, so please don't -- I'm addressing you because you happen to be -- but the thing is courtesy is wonderful and it is necessary. Saying things with a little bit of honey rather than in a confrontational manner also helps. So at the end of the day, this is how you have to work amongst yourselves. If you don't do this, there will be trouble and we'll have to start imposing deadlines. We'll say, sitting finished at 2.00, you have to hand the exhibit list by not later than 5.30, or 6.00. And we hate to do that. We hate to do that. But if there is going to be a delay, you should be in consultation with the other party. Please don't come forward and tell me, because I didn't know how to reach Ms. Vidovic. I don't know how to reach Ms. Vidovic, and I don't know how to reach you. But you shouldn't be in a position to say I don't know how to reach Mr. Jones and I don't know how to reach Ms. Vidovic. You should be in the position to know how to reach Mr. Jones and Ms. Vidovic, if need be. Maybe not directly, maybe through the registrar of the Tribunal, I don't know. It's up to you how you have built up the relationship together in prosecuting this case. But it's -- we don't want to hear this. I mean, if we want to approach you on something which is administrative, procedural, and which is necessary to be clear about before the next day, we get the registrar and he gets in touch with whoever needs to be contacted. I mean, and that's how it should be. But I don't expect Ms. Vidovic -- and I do understand her complaint saying at 10.30 finally -- no one should be waiting until 10.30 unless he has or she has shown her availability to wait. And if ultimately there are problems, we will see them here and we will tackle them here and we will act as arbiters, as I can assure you we can. But for the time being, please, we need -- or rather, you need to device a modus vivendi which will address the problems that you have with what you consider to be vagueness of the summaries provided by the Defence. The Defence -- I suppose you've heard what I had to say where you have complaints from the Defence regarding parts of the summaries which they consider to be vague. If you are in a position to elaborate on that, you should elaborate on that. What I'm saying is: If you don't create a modus vivendi among -- between yourselves which is conducive to a proper way of going ahead with this case, then we will intervene. But we have seen you cooperate in the past. We -- I don't even need to consult the other two Judges on this. We are 100 per cent sure that you approach these matters in the most responsible matter and that none of you really wants to back from cooperation. So let's hope that you will solve these problems and that when there are problems they will not be of obstacle to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, on behalf of the Prosecution we will contact the Defence if at the very late hour it's determined that the exhibit list will not be forthcoming as we had promised. But I should say we have always cooperated with them. When their exhibit list came in very late in the evenings, we contacted them. When it came in in the morning before cross -- cross-examination, we never raised a complaint to the Trial Chamber. In fact, we've been working with their schedule and we understand very much how intense this process is and we know that they weren't able to provide us with the exhibit list sometimes very late at night or early in the morning. And we've worked with that and we have never brought a complaint to the Trial Chamber. So I feel it's unfortunate that Madam Vidovic felt the need to raise it --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't push it further, now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, I've tried to calm the waters. I've tried to create an environment that would allow you to go around the table and talk and discuss and find a solution in the modus vivendi. To me, what I expected is for you and Madam Vidovic to stand up and tell us, We Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. have taken into consideration your suggestions and we will act responsibly, accordingly. Finished. And we don't want to hear --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And we will, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, that's finished. Then the matter is closed. Anything else? Not on this, I think we've already said that. All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Usher, please, could you please usher in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, Mr. Redzic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, too. Welcome back to this Tribunal and to this case. We are going to proceed with your evidence. You're not going to repeat the solemn declaration that you made yesterday; there is no need for that. But I'm just reminding you of the solemn declaration that you made yesterday. Madam Vidovic will proceed with her questions, and when we finish then we'll start with the cross-examination. We'll stop at 10.30 sharp or -- Madam Vidovic, or a little bit before. So we need to go until 10.30 because at 10.30 I have a meeting with two other Judges on something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have only a few short questions for Mr. Redzic. I almost completed my examination-in-chief yesterday. Yesterday we left it off at the moment when I wanted to show the D705 map to the witness. I would kindly ask the usher to show the witness this map. The number is D705.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, good morning. Before I ask you anything, I would like to greet you in this courtroom. Could you please look at this map once again. You saw it already once yesterday and yesterday we spoke about one of your conversations with Mr. Hodzic and also about a conversation with Mr. Becir Mekanic. You mentioned certain units, the units from Vlasenica that were billeted in Cerska and in Dzile. Now I would kindly ask you to show the Chamber on this map where Cerska and Dzile are located. If I may be of assistance. Can you look at Nova Kasaba and above Nova Kasaba look at the area there. You'll find Cerska there. Could you please mark the place if the felt-tip pen is at hand.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Redzic. And now the village called Dzile. This village is to the left. A bit below, Mr. Redzic, a bit below.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Redzic. You found it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise, my sight is not that good so it's very difficult to for me to find my bearings on this map.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: This will do. Thank you very much. Are these the places you mentioned yesterday and the places that you mentioned in your conversations with Mr. Mekanic and Mr. Hodzic and the places in which the Vlasenica units were?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Those were the enclaves in the Vlasenica municipality which were still free and where there was a large number of the population from Vlasenica. And this was the area where the local population still resided in great numbers.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'll go back to your conversation with Mr. Hodzic because this is where we left it off yesterday. You mentioned that he actually mentioned Hamed Salihovic to you. Did he tell you anything about his roles and his efforts in organising things on the ground?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did. Since I know Hamed in these conversations, Mr. Hodzic told me that this man, Salihovic, was very active in trying to organise all that and to see the decision taken of the ground with regard to the establishment of the subregion. I'm talking about the political and the military nature of that decision. On several occasions, he came to Cerska and to Konjevic Polje during the months of November, December, January, and until the fall of Cerska. He was there on a number of occasions and he tried to create and unify both the political and the military organisations in that area.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: These efforts on the part of Mr. Hodzic, were they fruitful? What did Mr. Hodzic tell you?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the -- his efforts were not fruitful because the conditions were not ripe for that. Nothing was there in place to implement the decision that was passed.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that after the fall of Cerska some other people came with Mr. Hodzic, that they arrived in Tuzla, and did you also speak to these people about the functioning of the subregion?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, Mr. Ferid Hodzic arrived in Tuzla after the fall of Cerska with a large group of soldiers, of men, from those areas. I spoke to the majority of these people. I wanted to hear their opinion as to whether the situation really was as had been conveyed to me by Mr. Hodzic. I must say that in any of these conversations and in every of them, these people described the situation in the same words and the story was always the same, whomever I heard it from.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that you were the president of the War Presidency of Vlasenica, with the seat in Tuzla. Provided that the subregion was formed in a legal fashion, would you be familiar with that fact?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Since I am a professional and I dealt with the tasks that were within my competence. And if I may, I would offer some suggestions. It is possible to forward a suggestion about formation of the subregion the same way certain proposals could come from the municipalities themselves. But at that time and in that area, such laws were in force - I believe they still are - that War Presidencies of any level or of any canton or any subregion are not able to verify and provide certification for certain suggestions. Only the War Presidency can do that, and then it had to be published in the Official Gazette. And never in any Official Gazette of Bosnia and Herzegovina had it been published, anything pertaining to such an organisation, be it of political or military nature pertaining to the subregion we mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: A very lengthy answer has already been provided, but this was clearly a leading question by Madam Vidovic. And I would ask again that we refrain because these are very, very important matters and the witness should be -- not be led.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Basically, I don't agree with you, Ms. Richardson. The question -- I mean, it wasn't phrased in the best of ways but it says: "Provided that the subregion was formed in a legal fashion," and that is assuming that -- for argument's sake that it was. Would you be familiar with that fact? So basically it's a question: What can you tell us about the legality or otherwise or the existence or otherwise of the subregion. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, precisely, Your Honour, but it seems that the question suggested that it was not leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It seems that we want to carry forward the antagonism that we detected this morning. So let's proceed. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I have a question just for clarification because I am not clear about your answer. You told us that War Presidencies of any level or any canton are not able to verify and provide certification for certain suggestions. Only the War Presidency can do that and then it had to be published in the Official Gazette. Now, at first you were referring to War Presidencies of any level or any canton, and then -- they cannot do anything. And then you spoke about the War Presidency who can do that. But what is the difference between both of these War Presidencies?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not -- I think not you, the witness. Yes, Mr. Redzic, you've heard what Judge Eser has asked you. Could you please explain to us the difference between the two kinds of War Presidencies that you seem to be referring to in your testimony. Which are these two categories of War Presidencies?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We are not dealing with two categories of War Presidencies. I believe I tried to explain any sort of War Presidency, and I concretely speak of municipalities; they had to be formed under war circumstances. Whether it was a political organisation at the level of the subregion or of the district, because later on it became the canton. No political body could be found by itself. Only the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina could do that. They were the only body that was able to accept or not certain nominations and they could provide suggestions as to the composition, and then it had to be confirmed by the Official Gazette as the candidates being accepted by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may, I tried to react earlier. The interpretation wasn't clear and the witness may correct me if I'm wrong. He said that the War Presidencies at the lower level that he specified, that -- those at the level of municipalities and subregions, they can only -- they could only be formed by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And I'm not certain as to whether the explanation was clear the second time. That was page 27, line 20 -- [In English] "Could be found by itself." [Interpretation] I guess the bodies couldn't appoint themselves, but rather they had to be appointed by the Presidency. So I have the question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Am I correct in my interpretation? Or rather, I can reiterate the question. Municipal War Presidencies or the subregional War Presidencies, could they appoint themselves or it had to be done from a higher instance by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I may explain again. War Presidencies up to the level of the subregion could not appoint themselves. They could offer suggestions as to their composition, but the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina could verify and they could appoint members to War Presidencies and then it could be confirmed within the Official Gazette, as in any other state where we have the rule of law.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, as the president of the Presidency in Vlasenica, did you see or hear of such a decision of the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As concerns my function within my competences it was to know about that, and I never saw it in any Official Gazette pertaining to the subregion.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just one other question or a couple. Working as a member of the War Presidency, did you have any contact with the authorities in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Did either you or your -- the people you worked with receive documents from the 2nd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with the seat in Tuzla, either you or your representatives or people that you worked with?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems to me there are two questions here: Whether we coordinated and participated in our activities with the authorities in Tuzla. In Tuzla at that time there was the district that was in existence, and it was a higher instance that united all the municipalities in that region plus the War Presidencies in exile from the subregion. We received all the documents from the district along the political lines as concerns the War Presidency. As concerns the corps and coordinating with the military authorities, in my testimony yesterday I mentioned that within the Vlasenica War Presidency there was a Mr. Fejzic who was the secretary for All People's Defence and anything pertaining to military documentation and cooperation with military authorities, there was his exclusive competence to deal with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday you told us that in the same building where your office was, there were also certain bodies of the town of Srebrenica. Do you know whether they had any correspondence with the authorities in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were in the same building. And logically speaking, we were within the same hallway, one office to the other. As concerns Vlasenica, it was a rather peculiar situations because there was a Mr. Mustafic Mirsad there who was a representative, and he would receive all documentation that would come in either pertaining to the military or the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I thank you, Madam Vidovic. Ms. Richardson. So, Mr. Redzic, now Ms. Richardson will be starting her cross-examination -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to apologise before my colleague takes over. I have a correction for the transcript. It states that Mr. Mirsad Mustafic coordinated in Vlasenica, but instead it was Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He has to -- the witness has to clear this up.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Please, can you clarify?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In my transcript here we have: "As concerns Vlasenica it was a rather peculiar situation because there was a Mr. Mirsad [Realtime transcript read in error "Musad"] Mustafic there" and he was representative -- I have here. I'm reading from the transcript. Now, was this correct or not? Was Mr. Mirsad Mustafic in Vlasenica or where was he operating as -- functioning as a representative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, the coordinator for Vlasenica was Mr. Fejzic and Mr. Mustafic was a commissioner for the municipality of Srebrenica and he had nothing to do with Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's Mirsad yeah, yeah, it's not Musad, but I had to read what I had there. So, yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Good morning, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Richardson, you are aware of the various points that we -- issues that we made clear to the Defence that we do not require any further evidence upon. So please be advised immediately that the moment you start touching on those issues unless you show cause why they are necessary to inquire about, I will stop you. Please concentrate on what is -- we said already is relevant for the remaining part of the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: May I ask for a further clarification and guidance by this Trial Chamber. I studied the decision on the first and second Defence filing pursuant to scheduling order dated 4th of July, 2005, in which it was addressed by Your Honours that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Should we have this in the presence of the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: We do not need to, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, usher, could you please escort the witness out of the courtroom for a little while and if we conclude this before the break we'll bring him in again. If not, we'll bring him in after the break. We have to discuss something which is of no interest to you, Mr. Redzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Those areas of Defence are clarified by Your Honours and indeed already also addressed in advance on Friday. I raised the question Friday that when it is an area of evidence, an area as defined by Your Honours, that should not preclude -- that should not stop the Prosecution for asking questions, otherwise defining such an area would be rather something like a factual finding that stopped the Prosecution for further asking questions to the witnesses. And according to it, I noticed when I received this decision by your Trial Chamber that the order clearly focussed on the Defence. So if I quote: "Your Honours hereby order that during the Defence case, the Defence shall not address the areas of evidence identified above except during the testimony of Defence witnesses," and then those two named today. So that's in alignment of my submission on Friday, and that's how I make an interpretation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are interpreting it correctly, Mr. Wubben. What we are telling you is the following: That there are areas where we have said we've heard enough. We don't need to hear more from the Defence. If you want to re-open these areas, you must satisfy this Trial Chamber first and foremost before you ask any questions what you intend to prove. And we will allow or disallow the questions accordingly, provided we consider that what you want to prove is relevant. Because now we have reached a stage after -- that you have concluded your case that there are things which are highly relevant, things which are highly irrelevant, and we will not allow you to proceed on matters which may satisfy your prosecutorial ego but which for us will create problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I hope I satisfy you that I don't form Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. such an ego. It's for me also the factual finding and you're right, Your Honours, it should be relevant. So my clarification, as I take it, is that the Defence shall not anyhow address such areas. And if the Prosecution shall have a question in that respect, it must be relevant, as all questions must be relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. If, for example, you think that when we say we don't want to hear anymore evidence on the genocide in Srebrenica in 1995, you think you want to re-open that chapter when we are telling the Defence it will not be re-opened, you will have to seek our permission before you do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is -- and if you justify your request, we will allow you to.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So that's the position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's a different approach --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are not in the -- you are not in the same position as the Defence. The Defence are being told rebus sic stantibus. As things are as present, we do not require any evidence from you on -- if the scenario changes because either the witnesses they bring change the scenario, which is as you both know is something that could happen very easily in any case. Okay. The witness which you bring forward, thinking that is going to testify in favour of your case suddenly stabs you in the back, I mean voluntarily or involuntarily. But that happens. It happened to you and it probably will happen to them. So at this point in time, you have to make an assessment. If you want to ask certain questions, I will hear the questions and I may come on you and say: I need to know why you are asking the question -- this question --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: That's clear, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because the situation as it is now is that there are several areas which for reasons that we tried to explain I think have been covered more than extensively. Some of these areas are highly relevant. Some of these areas are highly irrelevant. That's -- okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: It's clear. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's bring the witness in and at least use the first ten minutes. In the meantime, registrar, please do mark 54 minutes at this morning and -- yeah. We told you where we consider both of you and where we will ultimately be focussing in this case. And it's very simple. I mean, granted that there was military necessity to attack these villages, was there military necessity to burn down these houses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who did it? Was Mr. Oric responsible under 7(3) or under 7(1)? And only in the way of aiding and abetting. And as regards the first and second, you know what the parameters that we have established are. Believe me, Mr. Wubben and Mr. Jones and Madam Vidovic, it will be a clinical exercise on our part. If you think we are going to get lost in the labyrinth of other evidence that you would like to bring forward, forget it; we are not going to be -- get lost. Yes. Sorry. My apologies to you, Mr. Redzic, but we needed to discuss something which is of no interest to you and which doesn't concern you in any case. So Ms. Richardson will start and will finish in about 8 minutes -- I mean finish temporarily.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Redzic.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I would like to ask some questions about what you previously testified to, and I'd like to begin by talking about -- by asking you about the War Presidency that had been established in exile in Tuzla. Now, you mentioned that you were part of a War Presidency in exile on behalf of Vlasenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson, just to direct you, this is considered all relevant. So you can proceed along with all the questions you like on this area and what he testified subsequently about.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you -- could you tell us who were the other members of the War Presidency in exile on behalf of Vlasenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was the president of the War Presidency, and the other members were Ilija Jasarevic, Ramiz Kadric, Alima Trvalovic [phoen], and Midhad Fejzic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And what position did you hold?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, as the former president of the Executive Board I was assigned the task of -- the function of the president of the War Presidency in exile.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment, Ms. Richardson. Sorry to interrupt you but I see in the transcript all the names that he mentioned are practically not shown here. Let's start. I'll take this over for one minute. I'll get the names one by one. You told us you were president of this War Presidency?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go through the list of other members of this War Presidency. Next, after you. Say them one by one and slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ilijaz Jasarevic; Midhat Fejzic; Merima Telalovic; Ramiz Kadric. I can't recall the sixth member's name. If I may have a second. Mustafa Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, the other members that you just named, what were their positions? Did they have a particular title?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The role and purpose of that War Presidency was to receive the refugees, the Muslims who came from those areas, to provide some accommodation and to take care that the minimum levels of existence are offered as well as that all the citizens from the area of Vlasenica are registered so that it would be known in which municipalities they were at the then-free territory of the Tuzla district. If I have to, I can offer the names of all the municipalities and those were the competencies and the tasks we performed in that area and nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to the establishment of this War Presidency in exile, what laws were there to support this Presidency in exile?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a decree law in force. I believe it was P/92, tacitly regulated our relations as to who could be a member, and it was a good decree law and generally described the functions of the members, irrespective of their ethnicity, whether someone was a Serb or a Catholic or a Muslim. It was a good decree law, but when our people came to that area because we were exiled, we were not there of our own accord. And together with the representatives of the Vlasenica municipality, I tried to organise that body so that we could provide the minimum of existence for the people who found themselves there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: When was it that you organised the body? Could you give us a month, a date?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I mentioned that it was sometime around the end of April or the beginning of May. The proposal went to Sarajevo and the very appointment of the War Presidency happened in September or October of 1992 by the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And you can find that in the Official Gazette.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So in fact, you started working before the law came into -- was actually published in the gazette?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Laws were in force previously as well, irrespective of this decree law. If we refer to the laws of the former Yugoslavia and the then-Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, it prescribed the members of War Presidencies, except the title was different.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, let me stop you there. My question was: Did you in fact begin your work as the War Presidency prior to the law being published in the gazette in, I believe, September and October?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The nature of things was such, irrespective of whether the body was proclaimed or not. As the people who represented those people, we had the task to provide for the minimum of existence for those people there, as I stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have a break now. I need 30 minutes because I need to meet with Judge Robinson and Judge Liu. If it takes me longer, please bear with me. I'm not even going to have my coffee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, registrar. Registrar, would you just add another 12 minutes, please. Mr. Di Fazio, are you going to address that matter now or do you wish to, say, take a few minutes at the end?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I rather assumed I would do it after Ms. Richardson finished because I'm assured she's going to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. How much time do you require yourself?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I can probably deal with it in about 10 minutes, or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In a way which would call for reaction from the other side?

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Well, my guess is there will be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I need to calculate the time, obviously. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: I expect there would be some sort of reaction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, yes, Ms. Richardson, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, before the break you were testifying about the establishment of the War Presidency for Vlasenica, and you stated that you began your work of the War Presidency prior to the actual law being published in the gazette. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I've already said, we worked and it was our duty to do what was the most necessary for the refugees. While we worked, the name was not the War Presidency. We couldn't establish a War Presidency because the Presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina was the one that passed such decisions. We just initiated the establishment of it with a list of people who we thought should be members of the War Presidency. Our work was just the work of the people from the state institutions who were duty-bound to provide for the minimum conditions for the life and survival of those displaced people and refugees.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, the reason you established the War Presidency, or you proposed it, and you got together -- this group was because it was important because of the chaotic situation that yourself and the others found themselves in, in Tuzla, having left Vlasenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since the authorities in the district and the municipalities around Tuzla had to have somebody who would be a legitimate representative who would establish contact with humanitarian organisations and other international organisations that existed in the area in that given time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you went so far as to get the authorities in Tuzla to assign you a building where you could operate and work?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I have already stated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to Srebrenica, you mentioned that Mirsad Mustafic was a member of the War Presidency for Srebrenica. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't know whether he was a member of the War Presidency or not. I know that he existed in Tuzla as a commissioner. If there was a War Presidency in that area, then they were the ones who were responsible to authorise somebody in Tuzla who would coordinate things with the population because a number of people that had been displaced from Srebrenica were in that area. So his role was to coordinate work with the institutions of the political authorities, the military authorities, and he also looked after the refugees from Srebrenica who had arrived in Tuzla and in the surrounding areas in huge numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's get -- one moment, Ms. Richardson. Let's get this straight because I had understood all along that this person had nothing to do with Vlasenica; that was cleared up already. And that he was a representative for Srebrenica, but it wasn't clear in my mind that he was based in Tuzla and not in Srebrenica itself. So where was this Mirsad Mustafic residing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This gentleman resided in Tuzla. In my earlier testimony, I said that he covered the -- or he lived or he worked in a shed that the municipality of Tuzla gave to us to use for our work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And how did he receive information from Srebrenica, other than from the refugees -- from -- excuse me. How did he receive -- I'll rephrase the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because I don't think he said he received information from the refugees himself.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour -- I'll rephrase the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Mustafic, what was his role in Tuzla with respect to Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: His role was, by and large, similar to the role of other War Presidencies or bodies that worked at the time. He looked after the humanitarian aid, the accommodation of the refugees, and so on and so forth. And as a person representing the municipality of Srebrenica, I suppose that he received documents that were sent to him along the political lines or that some military bodies sent to him. There was nobody else from Srebrenica who was a legal representative of that municipality and who would be in a position to receive all such documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: With respect to his position, what law authorised him to represent Srebrenica of any -- if there was such a law?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Vidovic, what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the witness should be first asked whether he knows that at all, and then --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Knows what?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the question should be asked along the lines that Ms. Richardson put it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Knows what?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Whether he knows what was the law pursuant to which Mirsad was a commissioner, because Mirsad obviously did not hold the same position as the witness and he should be asked whether he knows that or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Objections are objections. Trying to testify instead of the witness I will not allow. This is basically nitpicking. I mean, it's -- when you say: "With respect to his position, what law authorised him to represent Srebrenica, if any, if there was such a law," it's a very valid question. If the witness is in a position to answer it, he will answer it. If he doesn't know about the law, if he doesn't know whether there was such a law, then obviously he's going to know -- to say "I don't know." Yes, Ms. Richardson, I will repeat the question for you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, the question that you need to answer is the following, and we are always referring to that person you mentioned before, Mirsad: With respect to his position that you described to us, what law authorised him to represent Srebrenica, if any, if there was such a law? So if you know of the existence of such a law, please tell us; if you don't know, please tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really wouldn't know. If there had existed such a law at the time, I'm sure I would know. I really don't know whether it was part of any law that this body could be established or that somebody could be authorised. I really don't know through what channels he received this position, whether through the War Presidency, the municipality of Srebrenica, or some state institutions or some district institutions. I really wouldn't be able to tell you because I never saw such a piece of paper. I was not interested in that, after all. If I had asked him what was the basis of his position, maybe he would have not liked it. It was the duty of every citizen, of every intellectual, from every municipality, from these parts and across Bosnia and Herzegovina to take a position and to help the refugees who had been expelled from their homes, whose families had been killed, and they had to provide these people and provide at least the minimum conditions for the survival of these retched people who had been through a lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And so, as you've stated, that it was the responsibility of individuals, this responsibility was carried out whether any law existed or not. Isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a responsibility. It was a duty of every citizen, of every intellectual, to help the people who had been through so much, as I've already said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you -- Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me rephrase it myself and then tell me whether this reflects what you want to tell us, because otherwise we will continue. Basically you are telling us that the situation was such that every -- those who were in the position to contribute felt that they had a moral obligation to do so and did not waste time in trying to see whether there was any legal obligation or laws which would regulate the way in which they would contribute. Would this reflect what you have testified?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the -- precisely what I said. The role and the task of every individual, of every intellectual, is not to look at the laws but to help people; subsequently, everything can be legalised. Everything can be put in a certain legal framework.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think it's clear enough now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And as you just stated that everything can be legalised and, of course, I imagine you mean later on it can be legalised once the work began, isn't that true for the subregion that was established?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my testimony, I have said that there may be proposals from the field and the body in the subregion has never been made part of any law of Bosnia and Herzegovina or anything that happened after the Dayton Accords once the Federation and the Republika Srpska were established. There is no paper trail of that sort. The initiatives could come from the local levels, from the subregional or cantonal levels, but it was well-known who was at the top and nobody could work on their own, independently. Nobody could appoint themselves to be minister. There was a procedure, there were elections, there were post-elections results, and based on those a parliament is formed, a government, and so on and so forth. The initiatives can start from the grass roots, but it was a well-known fact how things were legalised, how they were regulated at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: But my question was with respect to the subregion. You stated that individuals felt obligated to act, even if they were not authorised by the law at the time. And if I'm mischaracterising your testimony, please do tell me. With respect to the subregion, individuals who organised themselves and decided to act on behalf of the subregion, could they do that, in light of what you've already testified?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There may well have been an initiative. As far as the subregion is concerned, not for a single moment did it become operational. I told you what the key people, the people who had been proposed to represent the subregion told me. It really could not exist for a number of reasons, and if I need to repeat that, I will. It -- such a body could not exist within the -- that time frame. This subregion was supposed to be established in November when Cerska and Konjevic Polje had already been under attack by the aggressor. There was a lot of pressure from the enemy forces from all sides. Cerska and Konjevic Polje had already been cut off from Srebrenica; therefore, there was not even minimum condition in place for that. Let me not even start about the humanitarian situation, about people dying of hunger, children starving, elderly people not having medicines to help them and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, were you privy to all of the decisions that came out of Srebrenica, decisions made either by the War Presidency or the Territorial Staff of Srebrenica? Did you see these decisions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Will you locate it in a time frame, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
