utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Let me rephrase the question. When did you begin receiving information about the subregion?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already said that. The moment when free territories fell, like Cerska and Konjevic Polje, and when individuals like Ferat Hodzic and a large group of soldiers who came with him came. And only when I spoke with Ferat and others who arrived from the area, I learned that there really was an initiative of that sort. Your Honour, I am being asked very complex questions and in my answers I have to go to great lengths in order to explain things. I can't be brief, because if I'm brief then the Chamber will not get a real insight into what really went on in the area that we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: When we think that you are overdoing it or that you are giving us information that we don't require, we will stop you. Otherwise, go ahead unless -- unless we stop you. Thank you. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And so you did not receive information about this region until Cerska fell, which I believe you testified was about February of 1993. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, when these places fell and when the individuals from these places came, I was informed about those attempts, about the cries from people for help.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So you didn't receive any information about the subregion in 1992? I believe you can answer that with a yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And after his arrival in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And -- of course. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And after your arrival in Tuzla, I believe, in April.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, is that what you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Well, I'll rephrase the question, Mr. Redzic. You arrived in Tuzla in April of 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So from April of 1992 to February of 1993, when Cerska fell, you received no information about the subregion that had been established?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely no. You know what the siege looked like. Even the international community could not enter to secure the minimum conditions for the people there to survive. How could I have known? There were individuals who could come through, but I didn't know about it. I knew some things about Vlasenica and its territory, but concerning the things prior to -- to the fall of Cerska, which was a relatively short interval, and when other people came, as I said, this is when I learned about some of their attempts and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, with respect to Mr. Mustafic, when did he arrive in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say exactly. I don't know the date, but he participated in the work and he was in the same locality where people from Vlasenica, Srebrenica, Zvornik. He was also there, but we shouldn't mention Mr. Ibranic only -- sorry, Mr. Mustafic. There were other people from Srebrenica who were trying to do something to help the people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: What about the -- what are the names of the other people?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For example, the general manager of the utility company from Srebrenica, Mujo Muratovic, if I'm not mistaken. Then Adip Dzozic who were at the disposal to help the people since he was an intellectual with a high degree of education and he offered his services to provide the minimum conditions for those people, to help in that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Getting back to Mr. Mustafic, you said you can't remember when he came. Could you narrow it down to the time of year. Was it the summertime? Was it in the fall that he came to Tuzla? And was it in 1992?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really can't remember the period when he came, but I previously mentioned other people who also worked there. And I used to see this gentleman on occasion, but I can't put it in the exact time context, whether that was the end of April or beginning of May.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you can't say if it was 1992 or 1993?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe it was 1993. It was already very late. I believe it was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right. And you testified that he received reports from Tuzla. Could you tell us what types of reports -- sorry, from Srebrenica, excuse me. Could you tell us what types of reports he received?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said earlier, he received no information from Srebrenica. You probably heard me say that earlier. He received written information along the political lines from the institutions of the republic, the canton, and the district, and partially from the military domain. He received absolutely no information from Srebrenica itself because there was no open channel in existence. I don't know of any single document that he may have received from Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: So any information he received from Srebrenica about Srebrenica -- I'll rephrase the question. Was he -- did the information he received, was that about the conditions in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know. I do know that he received some documents, but as to what those documents were, what was in them, I really can't say.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you mentioned that the information were partially from the military domain. What military domain are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated a minute ago, information came along the political lines and I would see the people who would bring them in and then I -- by -- because of that I knew that it came from the military because they were brought by couriers who wore uniforms from the corps, from the military structures. They would bring papers, but I can't say anything as to their content because I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And where you -- you testified that couriers were -- would come and they wore uniforms from the corps. What area did they come from, do you know, with the couriers? Where did they originate? Was it from Sarajevo or Tuzla or Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a hierarchy. It would be illogical for it to come from Srebrenica. Those people came from the headquarters of the corps and the distance to our offices was 1 kilometre. They came from there, from the building of the corps to our building where the refugee population that was trying to do something for the general -- more general population was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the information that he received from the corps, did you -- did he discuss this with you?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As for the military issues, I am quite ignorant about that. I'm not an officer. I had a person who was tasked with coordinating the military matters. I had other tasks. I had to find accommodation. I tried to provide the minimum conditions that I mentioned, so I never dealt with that and I was not even interested in what it was that Mr. Mustafic would receive.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you familiar with members of the War Presidency of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with whether he was aware that there was a War Presidency because the composition changed, as you know, and whether he was aware of the existence. And if he was, when did he become aware of it --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- to start with --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And I'll take it in stages and steps --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then I think it's better.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, were you aware that Srebrenica in May -- I'll rephrase. Were you aware that Srebrenica had established a War Presidency sometime after May of 1992?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't talk about that issue, one of the reasons being that there was complete paralysis and the siege, inability to communicate concerning Sarajevo and the Official Gazettes. They would often be published a year later in relation to the date they were put -- that certain laws were put into force. Some Official Gazettes I saw a full year later, that includes Srebrenica and other municipalities in particular. So I can't say much about that time and about the members themselves. I'm not familiar with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's because you limited your question to May or just after May in 1992. That's why I suggested in the first place it should be put in pieces. First question: Were you aware at -- during this time that you were in Tuzla of the existence of a War Presidency in Srebrenica? Answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say yes or no. I really don't know about it because that territory was cut off and they had no open channels to communicate. Perhaps at the very beginning when the siege was relatively incomplete, but later on I wasn't particularly interested in the delay with the Official Gazettes. But as concerns this month of May or the end of April, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget the gazette, forgot whether -- I'm not asking you whether you became aware at any time of a proclamation, official proclamation published in the government gazette or not, published in the government gazette, that set up the War Presidency in Srebrenica. I'm asking you a very simple question: During your stay in Tuzla or after your arrival in Tuzla, did you at any time become aware that a War Presidency had been set up, in other words existed, in Srebrenica? Not whether it had been legally set up, whether it had been published. Did you hear of a War Presidency in Srebrenica at any time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By the sheer nature of things, whether it was legal or not, I would presume that people there tried to do something. And when discussing it with people on the street, I learned about a War Presidency and it only seemed logical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So then I'm giving him back to you. I will not ask him any further questions on this, obviously, but I just wanted to try and get this out.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I do appreciate that, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, I'd like to ask you a series of questions about your meetings that you testified to on examination-in-chief, the meetings that you had at the regional level with the various municipalities including Srebrenica and Bratunac. Now, you testified that you had meetings with Ibran Mustafic. Would that be correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only with him but with all the representatives of the aforementioned five municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you -- with respect to Srebrenica, those are -- that is where my questions will be limited to for this time. You also met with Besim Ibisevic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Besim Ibisevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Ibisevic, excuse me. Thank you. And he also represented Srebrenica, both of them?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated yesterday, the meetings included five municipalities and were attended by the presidents of the Executive Boards of the municipalities and of the SDA of those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And the goal of the meeting --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: The goal of the meetings that you held were to determine exactly what was occurring politically as well as in the sense of security in the municipalities?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. At that moment we had several enemies beginning with the League of Communists and the army and the Serb people who were armed. Our role was to gather the correct information as to what was happening in the territory of the subregion and at the level of the entire state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as I mentioned yesterday. And meetings often covered that as well. So the purpose of the meetings was to deal not only with Srebrenica but as well as with Bratunac, Zvornik, Vlasenica, a part of Sekovici because it was almost 100 per cent Serb territory with Serb population. But the role was to gather information from all those territories and one of the key roles was to attempt to reinstate peace so as not to see Bosnia and Herzegovina go up in flames so that the things that did happen and the things that we are sitting here because of wouldn't take place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And you relied on the representatives from the municipalities for information about their particular municipalities. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Not only myself but others relied on that information and I, myself, submitted information pertaining to Vlasenica. But as to how I gathered that, it was dictated by logic. I couldn't be present in every square metre of the Vlasenica territory; it had over 507 square kilometres. But we had people in the field who were tasked with monitoring the situation and the events, movements of various groups, including the military and other. And then they would forward that information to us. And within a municipal or a subregional body, we would discuss the issues. We would try to find a way out. We tried to calm the situation and we kept on saying that no -- no provocation should be done on part of the Muslims because that would only bring about retaliation by the other party.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you also discuss in this meeting of the various representatives what the representatives were doing in their municipality in terms of meeting with the other side, meaning the Serbs, and the SDS, as they were themselves trying to resolve the situation, the security situation, in their municipality?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. That was no secret. The same thing that was done in my municipality was done in the neighbouring municipalities. We tried, and the Serbs were already on their way in organising military and political institutions, so the military came out of their barracks and a part of it returned from Slovenia and Croatia. They were not in the barracks but out in the field and on the roads. And we couldn't expect Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. anything but to receive Serb demands and to try to meet them to avoid the war, murders, and destruction that took place. So it is true. I in my municipality, as well as representatives from other municipalities, we did everything to bring about peace, so as not to see the Muslim people destroyed because by that time the tanks were already out and they started killing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON

"The representatives of two national parties from Srebrenica met on 21st September, 1991, with the goal of settling the large number of inter-ethnic problems. Zmigo), and Milenko Canic made up the SDS delegation. The Serbian representatives put the following issues on the agenda: The allocation of lots for the construction of privately owned homes in the town; the dismissal of Serbian employees from some Srebrenica enterprises; the appointment of directors of elementary school, the removal of military files from the municipal building, and failure to send call-up papers to Serbian recruits for regular military service," and I will just end there for now. In other words, meeting with members of the SDS trying to come to agreements about the difficulties they were having?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle is the same as in the municipality of Vlasenica. The Serbian representatives of the SDS and the municipal institutions from the same party sought any possible way to find a cause and reason to use and to carry out their activities. What is mentioned here is really ugly, and that is that the Serbs have been sacked from some companies that directors were being appointed. Yes, after the elections, after the authorities were established according to the votes that they won, they had to distribute positions amongst themselves; that is nothing new under the sun. They were multi-party elections and it is only logical that the parties could appoint people to the positions according to their cut in power. The mobilisation is also mentioned here, and that is no secret. I've already spoken about that. It was our task and role to prevent the mobilisation of Bosnians and Herzegovinians irrespective of their religion, colour of the skin, or race. Bosnia-Herzegovina and its leaders did not allow any Bosnian or Herzegovinian to go to the front lines in Croatia and to kill the Catholics or any other peoples there. Really, everything like that happened in Vlasenica to a somewhat smaller extent because I was somewhat wiser. However, I did mention the blockades, the ban on the exploitations of forests, and I don't even want to mention the mobilisation. I told the Serbs: You Serbs can mobilise as much as you want but this is illegal. I'm not sending my people to wage wars outside my country.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you want to put any further question on this, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, I just didn't want to interrupt.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS

utterances.text: Now, Mr. Redzic --

utterances.text: Now, Mr. Redzic, did it also come to your attention from Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ibisevic --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- Ibisevic that they had established in Srebrenica a National Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. That was provided for by law. utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: And this National Defence Council consisted of members of the SDA as well as members of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To your knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: To your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, absolutely. It was the president of the Municipal Assembly, the president of the Executive Board, the commander of the Territorial Defence, the chief of police, and members of the clubs of -- members of parliament representing those parties that made up the authorities at that level.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I don't want to dwell on this point, but I'd like you to turn to page 38 --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, do you see there are a list of nine individuals and it starts with the first name Besim Ibisevic, and it also lists Ibran Mustafic which is number 8 on this list. As you glance at this, does this confirm what you know of? Can you -- I'm not sure if the witness can hear me.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you were listening to me, I said that the National Defence Council is provided for as a body and I told you who such a council was made up of. The president of the municipality, the president of the Executive Board, the chief of police, and representatives of all the parties as well as the head of the Territorial Defence. This was provided for by the law. This was done while there was still peace and where -- when there was a rule of law. I'm mentioning this because this stems from the laws of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were in effect then and which would continue to be in effect in the Federation and in the part where the political authorities and the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina were in power. You didn't say anything different to what I explained to you about the make-up of the National Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, please don't argue with counsel. Counsel will put questions to you and you try to answer the questions. And the question basically I think you have derailed it a little bit. The question was a very simple was; it was inviting you to look at this list and confirm to Ms. Richardson whether this corresponded to what you knew at the time. This is basically it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, absolutely. There was a rule of law, laws were in place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's move, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: After all Besim Ibisevic, who was the president of the municipality, is writing this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Indeed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Redzic, did it come to your attention from the representatives of Srebrenica, Mr. Ibisevic and Mr. Mustafic, that in fact there were individuals in Srebrenica who had weapons?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what side you are referring to. If you're referring to the Serbian side, then the question is pointless. At that moment, the Serbian people on the 11th of April was armed to the tooth. They had weapons located around Srebrenica, Vlasenica, Bratunac, across the subregion and across Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think we need -- because otherwise we will again deviate into areas that we don't want to hear about. Your question was: "Now, Mr. Redzic, did it come to your attention from the representatives of Srebrenica, Ibisevic and Mustafic, that in fact there were individuals in Srebrenica who had weapons?" utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Muslims or the Serbs. Because if it's the Serbs, I don't think we need to hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in fact, my question -- I was actually going to qualify my question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I was talking -- excuse me, Mr. Redzic, for not being clear. I was talking about Muslims having weapons in Srebrenica, and when I say "Srebrenica," the town and the surrounding villages, the municipality of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Did you have information as to whether they were armed or not? This is the whole question, whether the Muslim population were armed or not, from these two persons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to our information, the Muslim people had hunting rifles that had been obtained legally, and there were also some individuals who had purchased weapons. And I can say this openly, that these weapons were purchased from the Serbs. We're talking about a small number of weapons that had been purchased by the Bosniaks, who did not have the money to purchase weapons in huge numbers. And there was nowhere from weapons to be obtained from.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Who did you obtain this information from? Did you obtain this information from these two persons, from Ibisevic and the other person, Mustafic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At our meetings we analysed the situation, we discussed such cases. There were people who did not understand what the war was and what force we were facing. In Vlasenica we had information only of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Forget Vlasenica --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- the weapons that had been issued, the hunting rifles and such weapons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, we're talking of Srebrenica and we wouldn't like to hear any more about the situation in Vlasenica. utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what period you're referring to. If you're referring to this late period around the 11th of April and later, I really did not have any information at the time because at the beginning of April we had our last contact with the people who were in those municipalities. In the period leading up to that period, we used to meet and every president of the Executive Board and the president of the Municipal Assembly had to be privy to the situation in their respective areas, how many inhabitants, how many cows, meadows, and so on and so forth. utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which April are you talking about? April 1992 or April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1992.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Did you learn, Mr. Redzic, that individuals in Srebrenica had been smuggling weapons and selling them -- smuggling weapons into Srebrenica and had been selling them?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Sorry, usually of course it would be my colleague who would raise an objection. But there are two points, really, finding, or however one wants to describe it, number 10, was that the Bosnian Muslim capacity in Srebrenica was largely dependent on weapons that could be captured from the Bosnian Serb forces. I'd like to have -- the Prosecution is seeking to challenge that finding because that has all kinds of implications, firstly. And secondly, generally, I don't see the relevance otherwise of this line of inquiry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What are you trying to prove, Ms. Richardson?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That the Muslims were militarily superior to the Serbs --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, absolutely not, Your Honour. In fact, I'm just doing a cross-examination in relation to the examination that was conducted whereby it was stated that the Muslims had no weapons and I'm just seeking to establish whether in fact this was in fact true, not that they were superior. But I think it is relevant that there were weapons, not that they were superior.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Jones.

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: The seniority is finding number 9. Finding number 10 is that Bosnian Muslim military capacity was largely dependent on weapons that could be captured from Bosnian Serb forces. That's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Wubben.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I strongly object to the word "finding."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's not a finding. But let's not give importance to words which are not -- which are not important. It's not a finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I do think it's relevant that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's relevant that we are aware of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you want to prove that the Muslims could defend themselves with the weapons they had?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If you don't want to prove that, if you're not seeking to prove that, forget it and move to your next question. No one seems to have even imagined for a moment that anyone was taking a position that the Serbs had all the weaponry and that the Muslims had absolutely nothing, not even one gun; no one has suggested that. I mean, we -- I think you --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to face the reality of the situation that if you are living in town and you are surrounded and you are being attacked from the air and from artillery from the hills, and the way you are you cannot defend yourself with shotguns.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I am seeking to establish that in fact there were weapons present in Srebrenica prior to the attacks --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's granted. I don't think you need to prove it. I think we are satisfied that there were a lot of weapons in Srebrenica as well, but we are also satisfied for the time being that the -- if you need to address the point that the Muslims could defend themselves in Srebrenica and in the surrounding villages with the weapons that they had, yes, I will allow you to do that by all means.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: That's fine, Your Honour, I will move on to that point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We never took the position that the Muslims had no weapons; we just the position that for the time being we don't need to address this matter any further because I think we've heard enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, could I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Could I just have a moment?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if it is the case that it is not necessary to explore how many weapons were in Srebrenica, then I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry. Try to understand the message that we tried to send loud and clear to both of you. After the end of the case of the Prosecution in a way and in more than one way, the case has crystallised itself and there are some issues that are extremely relevant and some issues that are no longer relevant, in our opinion. And please try to address those issues which you as Prosecution need to address, and which the Defence needs to address because of the way in which the case for the Prosecution has developed. The case and the guilt of the accused under 1 and 2 certainly does not depend -- Ms. Richardson --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yes -- yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- for the purposes of Counts 1 and 2, certainly we don't need to talk about the weapons that the Muslims had in Srebrenica. As regards Counts -- the other two Counts, 3 and 5, I told you: What -- this is going to be a clinical performance. What is relevant is whether at the moment of the attack it was militarily necessary to burn down those places or not, number one; secondly, who did it; thirdly, there is an allegation that the accused may have been present in one or more of these occasions, what does his presence mean if he was present at all; fourthly, he is being charged under 7(1) and 7(3), okay. So under 7(1) it's limited to aiding and abetting and under 7(3) it's whether he had effective control. And also, we invite you not to waste much time on whether he had a de jure superior -- there was a de jure superior/subordinate relationship or whether it was a de facto one. Because if there is or there was a de facto one, we will proceed. So this is why I'm making it very clear: Don't get yourself lost in the labyrinths of the many issues that you have in this case that may seem very important on the face of it, but we may -- which we may ultimately throw overboard as if they have never been presented. This is the naked truth. Otherwise, if you don't want to take heed, both of you, I'm telling you where, in our opinion, you need to concentrate and we are telling them where they need to concentrate because after the end of the Prosecution case and the throwing away of two of the counts, what's left is very obvious. And you have either proved your case or you haven't. So at the end of the day, how important is it for us to know whether the population in Srebrenica, the Muslim population in Srebrenica had just shotguns or more than shotguns or had .005 weapons per capita or more than one weapon per capita? Is it going to change anything? Because at the end what is going to count is: Was there a military necessity to burn down all those houses? That's it. And we are not going to ask ourselves many more questions beyond that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may, and I'm sure you would stop me if I again go into the area --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't mean to stop you to interrupt you. I mean to stop you only to address you to what we are telling you should be concentrating upon. And when I say "we are telling you," we are not telling you to concentrate on this or -- because that's your business, just as we don't tell the Defence how to conduct their business. But there are certain areas that are not more important than others, but there are certain areas which are not going to make a difference. So why keep addressing them?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And again, it's because of lack of -- we seem to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, you take your time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- of clarity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I didn't impose on you any time limit when this finish this witness. And I do appreciate that you have certain concerns. However, let me make it clear, if you still believe that this importance of how much weapons the Muslim populations of Srebrenica had is relevant and important, just tell me and I will let you put the questions. That means that I will also allow the Defence to open up that chapter again.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Just a moment, again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's have a break and in the meantime you will have time to consult. 25 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have lost your --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Oh. Thank you, Your Honour, I do apologise to the Bench for my lack of robing here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that could have cost you a lot. So let's -- did you discuss, by any chance, with Mr. Di Fazio how much time to leave him?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I should be done in no more than 15 to 20 minutes, even less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Let's proceed. I was only concerned to make sure that Mr. Di Fazio will have his time, in which case we would have provided ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, with respect to your question that you asked prior to the break whether the Prosecution still believe it was important to elicit evidence of weapons by the Muslims, it's our position that it is still relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we consider it not to be. So move to the next question, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Redzic, you testified yesterday that you had made visits to various Serb villages, accompanied by members of the SDS or members of the Serb authorities jointly to inspect villages. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went together with the president of the Municipal Assembly, Mr. Stankovic, who is a Serb by nationality. We didn't go there to inspect, but we went there together with the police because at that time there were already important issues and problems there, created by some individuals that I had mentioned yesterday and it occurred in several localities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And you also testified that -- when you were asked on examination-in-chief about whether or not Mr. Ibisevic had visited -- had been told, excuse me, about weapons -- excuse -- maybe ... Perhaps I should just rephrase the question, and I'll read from the transcript and you can listen to my question. It will derive from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. what you said yesterday. You testified in examination-in-chief regarding what Mr. Ibisevic had said in his book, and I am reading from page 45 of the transcript. It says that: "Simo Jusic from the village of Poznanovic a member of the Municipal Assembly told me that there had been shooting from the night before. The Bosniaks in the village spent the night in the open, guarding the village. He also told me that Serbs from the village of Fakovici had a store of weapons and ammunition stash in an abandoned schoolhouse near the village of Ruljevici in the municipality of Bratunac. The Serbs had received arms from JNA. The Bosniaks had seen military lorries arriving in the village. I promised Simo I would personally go to Ruljevici and check whether there were arms there. The Bosniaks had to know the truth." Now, my question is with respect to what was quoted to you from the book is regarding rumours that various Serbs had weapons. And my question is: Is it a fact that there were rumours on both sides about weapons? In other words, there were rumours that Serbs had weapons and there were rumours that Bosniaks had weapons, or Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were rumours that the Bosniaks did possess weapons. As for the Serb people, it is true, and it comes clear from all the analysis done so far by the international community and our analysis, that the Serbs much earlier had transferred their weaponry from the TO and it was distributed by the SDS and the JNA. So there was no misinformation there pertaining to the arming of the Serb villages. As concerns the Muslim villages, I claim here that of course there were exceptions but the Bosniak people did not possess weapons, almost none.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would like the witness to be shown -- we're still using Defence Exhibit 6 --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: 690, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: It's page 66 of the English, and the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- it's page 240.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Now, I will read from page 66. This page, which is an excerpt of the book of Mr. Ibisevic: "National Defence Council, Municipal Assembly of Srebrenica, 4th April, 1992, excerpts. Minutes of the meeting."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could you please read slowly, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: "The teams appointed at the preceding session of the council to visit a part of municipal territory have reported to the council at the National Defence Council session of 4th April, 1992: 1, the first task team consisted of Besim Ibisevic, chairman of the Municipal Assembly of Srebrenica; and Miodrag Stanisavijevic, commander of the municipal territory defence of Srebrenica, visited the villages of Fakovici, Skelani, and Bajina Basta. It was established on the site in Fakovici that no JNA units or paramilitary units were present at that location." Now, having read the minutes from the national council meeting, do you agree that they went out to the village of Fakovici and determined that there were no JNA units present or paramilitary units present at that time?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on his information and what he wrote in the book, I include that with the person he mentioned here, a Mr. Miodrag, they went around to see certain locations, as reported to the Municipal Assembly. He found a group of people there who were located there and who were guarding a warehouse full of weaponry and ammunition. By mentioning that, he said that in the area of Ruljevici, Fakovici, and Skelani, large numbers of people were seen wearing weapons and uniforms of drab-olive colour. He mentions in the book what he saw and what his conclusions were. It is true that he went with a Serb who was the TO commander of Srebrenica, and they saw this with their own eyes, and even that Serb himself was appalled. And he asked him, How did you dare go through that area?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, what you've just stated is clearly inconsistent with what Mr. Ibisevic has said in the meeting. Is there any indication, as you look at what he has said about Fakovici, that there was a group of people guarding a warehouse full of weaponry and ammunition? If you just look at that first paragraph, is that mentioned in the minutes anywhere?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not mentioned here, but that's probably for some other reasons --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, that's all I wanted to know. Now, if you go to the -- what is listed as Roman numeral V, it's page 67 on the English version: "Ibran Mustafic, chairman of the Municipal Assembly" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Slowly. One moment, we need to catch up with you a little bit. I think you need to go to the next page. Is it the same page?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour -- well it should be the next page, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I will start reading if you've located this -- the portion that I'm going to refer to. Now: "Ibran Mustafic," and I'm reading from page 67, number 5, or Roman numeral V, "chairman of the Srebrenica Municipal Assembly, Executive Committee, visited yesterday the villages of Miletici, Derventa, Zutica, and Suceska. He stated that there had been no excesses except for tension noticeable in both ethnic groups." There's no mention that Mr. Mustafic, as you read this meetings report, there's no mention that Mr. Mustafic came across any weapons by Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are wasting our time, Ms. Richardson, and you don't want to listen to me. We are not interested in April of 1992 --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And we are not interested in May of 1992. We are interested only in what happened on those days when allegedly, according to Counts 3 and 5, there was wanton destruction. That's what we are interested in. You don't seem to understand, and you still seem to be more interested in losing yourself in these nice labyrinths of irrelevant -- does it mean to say that if there were no weapons in April, then therefore there were no weapons in May?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: No, your --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And in June and in July and in August and in September and as we go into January of 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, you are absolutely correct, it does not say that at all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead, go ahead, go ahead --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: We have heard testimony from this witness that there were Serb --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: -- and they had an enormous amount of weaponry when they visited, and this is what they were able to observe. And this is a matter of credibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Of course. All right, if it's a matter of credibility, yes, you may -- you can address it. If it's a matter of credibility, I won't stop you for sure. If it's a matter of credibility. If it's about trying to show what was the position in April of 1992, I mean, forget it, because we are not interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, if I may add to this. Perhaps it might be for the coming proceedings supportive that whenever there is a -- questions towards the Prosecution: Is it relevant or not, and Prosecution confirm to it that Prosecution also should take the floor to give the reasons why it is relevant because this might be a misunderstanding. Is only relevant for that purpose but I know in advance that Ms. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: Ms. Richardson included that credibility issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, okay. But I didn't know. I wasn't aware of that. And obviously she can proceed in as far as credibility is concerned. Otherwise, pushing the point forward as to what was the position militarily in April 1992, come on.

utterances.speaker: MR. WUBBEN
utterances.text: This is in addition, and it might be productive for the coming proceedings --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. Yes, Ms. Richardson, my apologies to you. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, you mentioned that -- I don't have any other questions with respect to this document. You mentioned that there was no communication with Srebrenica during the period of 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to answering your question, if I may, could I stay with item 7, please --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed there is an invitation to the Serbs to return to their homes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Having in mind --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. Mr. Redzic, you answer the questions that are put to you and not what you would like to answer. Please, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll just rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Was there any communication that you know of with Srebrenica in 1992 while you were in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 1992 is an entire year --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Yeah. Your Honour, I'll be more precise.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: From May of 1992 to December of 1992.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There was some sort of communication and exchange of information but only once Muslims were expelled from those areas. The only source of information were those people. I have to correct myself somewhat. There was even a telephone line there up until mid-June 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Were you aware that individuals were -- in Srebrenica were contacting family members in Tuzla and Sarajevo via radio communication?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say anything about that. I can't say yes or no. I wasn't present to any of the conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So you're telling us that you never heard that in spite of what the circumstances and the situation was in Srebrenica, people in Srebrenica were being -- were -- had the possibility of contacting their relatives via radio in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps in the later phase when communication was open via ham radio operators and so on. But at the very beginning until mid-June 1992 until the end of 1992, it was almost completely blocked. There were no information -- there was no physical communication as well as any other sort of communication.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. As you know, when did this ham radio possibility surface? When did it happen? When did it start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wasn't following that closely at the time, since I lived some -- under such conditions that I had no radio or a TV set as a refugee in Tuzla. I was accommodated with the rest of the people, and I can't recall the exact date when such radio ham operators communication could have been established.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Richardson.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: In your discussions with Ferat Hodzic, did he tell you that Serb prisoners had been taken in Cerska during an operation conducted by the Muslim forces?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is about Mr. Hodzic. We didn't discuss that topic and I don't know of such information.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So you're not showing the 328, 329? All this is --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, in light of what Your Honour's ruling has been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Right. That's why --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHARDSON
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm soliciting an explanation, that's all. Yes, is there re-examination, Ms. Vidovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have only a couple of questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Redzic, you held a position in the municipality of Vlasenica even before the war. Were you ever relieved of that duty before December 1992?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Legally speaking, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that intellectuals and management from Srebrenica and Vlasenica as well as other municipalities in the Podrinje area were under a great pressure by the SDS and did that have any impact on the fact that they were the first that had to leave?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The old saying goes that the snake is best killed if its head is cut off first. So they removed intellectuals first and whoever remained, they were eliminated and they never managed to reach the free territories.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: My purpose was actually the following. Were there any intellectuals left in the villages, either in Vlasenica or Srebrenica, who would be familiar with the legal regulations of who would establish appropriate organs?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. This is the country -- there are many illiterate people. If one is to look into the statistics, the figures of illiteracy are very high.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Concerning the book, we showed you a paragraph pertaining to the 3rd of April, and it forms part of this book of Mr. Ibisevic concerning the incident in Ruljevici. He described it there. Is it true that you learned about that incident from him?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as well as for other -- or about other incidents. It was on the eve of the war and it was becoming clear what was ahead of us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When the Prosecutor was questioning you about the excerpt from the minutes, that was the last document shown to you, you said there were other reasons because of which the minutes were as they were here. Could you please tell the Chamber what those reasons were.

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. Those moments -- those reasons occurred a year before the war. Around and in Srebrenica, the situation was similar as it was in Vlasenica. When one goes through the items, the council invites the Serbs to return to their work posts and to their homes because by that time they have already seceded parts of the Srebrenica municipality by forming another municipality with the seat in Skelani. The Muslims, the Bosniaks, who were members of that body did their utmost to preserve peace there and they were not in any favour of any secession or removing members of families, children, women, across the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: Another question pertaining to that. On the 4th of April, 1992, was there pressure exerted on the Muslims, in particular people in positions such as Mr. Ibisevic, or you who were involved in the functioning of municipal organs in order to accept certain decisions? Did there exist such a pressure to accept or disregard something?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In order to clarify something to the Chamber, the SAO Birac was proclaimed, and in the Municipal Assembly of Vlasenica, by the end of February, an item was imposed on the agenda in order to vote on the decision of the parliament and that Vlasenica be included within the SAO Birac. After that the Serbs gained majority, particularly when I mentioned the electoral results, and they forced us to split Vlasenica between the three municipalities I mentioned. Otherwise, they threatened to use tanks. And me and a negotiating team had to accept that, otherwise I wouldn't be sitting here before you today.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: To clarify and link it up with the document, the essence of the question was the following: Was there any pressure exerted on the Muslim -- Muslims who were in positions of power in order to accept the division?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely. They were ready to eliminate us, to kill us, and we had to accept, irrespective of what a particular demand or request was, we had to accede to it to save our lives.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: What is it that you had to do?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had to sign any paper they would put before us.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Mr. Redzic, I would have some questions to you. Yesterday you have been asked with regard to the relationship between the different commanders in the field, and you answered that there has been some conflicts between them, that there has been animosity between them. Could you give some names with regard to these commanders who had some conflicts with each other?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday I tried to explain this. It was Mr. Becir Mekanic and Mr. Fadil Turkovic who were with the Zulfo from Suceska. There were huge conflicts there as I have explained. Mr. Mekanic abandoned the area and went to Cerska, the free territory of Vlasenica, and towards the end of October he arrived in the territory of Tuzla. There was a clash, there was animosity, there was a fight over control. And these people were not commanders; they were just people who enjoyed certain reputation among the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. people and that's why they controlled and commanded, if you will, those people, although there were -- there was no subordination as such at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: At this moment I was not asking for subordination. It was your own term to speak of commanders. Now, you mentioned Zulfo Tursunovic so far as the only name. Was there a special reason why you mentioned him in particular?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about these areas because they are close to the area where Mr. Becir Mekanic and Fadil Turkovic were. The latter was the commander of the police earlier. They hailed from the area, they exerted influence among the people, and that area bordered on some parts of Suceska, and Suceska according to my information, that's where Zulfo was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: But my question was whether besides Zulfo Tursunovic there was any other name mentioned with regard to commanders who had some conflicts with each other. Who else had conflict with -- conflicts with Zulfo Tursunovic?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Mekanic, the one that I mentioned, he also was one of those. Ferid Hodzic as well. There were no command relationships over there. Those were just individuals who organised themselves in order to protect their homes, to protect the people who were fleeing. That was the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, what have been the question, the issues, on which they had some conflicts? What was the reason? And why did they quarrel with each other?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably who would bear the title of the commander; that was the key issue I suppose, probably.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Only with regard to the title of commander, nothing else?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. There might have been something else that was at stake, but I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: We don't want to speculate, but what time within -- between April 1992 and March 1993, what special time are you referring to that there had been animosities or conflicts between different people leading certain groups? Let me put it in a very vague [sic] way, perhaps. What time are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about Becir Mekanic and Fadil Turkovic and I'm referring to the early stages of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina up to sometime towards the second half of September, when I'm talking about the two of them and Zulfo. And I also said that Ferid Hodzic never recognised Mr. Naser Oric or anybody else. Indeed, there were multiple clashes. There was more discussion about what would rule, who would be commander. Then whether defence would be organised properly and whether people would be saved. The territorial separation between Cerska and Konjevic Polje, which were separated from Srebrenica and from the free territory of Vlasenica where Fadil Turkovic and Ibisevic were. We're talking about a distance of 30 kilometres, 30 kilometres from one place to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: And with regard to your own function you have mainly been involved in, let's say, civil matters to care for refugees and things like this. Have you ever been involved in any strategic or military decision with regard to attacks which may have been performed? Have you ever been involved in military affairs during your time in Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not. The military has its laws and regulations; the civilian authorities have theirs. I was a refugee. No local community would be -- would allow me to engage in any strategy, be it military or a civilian one. My task and the task of my colleagues was to look after the refugees, to look after the bare necessities for their survival. That was all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: I don't want to challenge your own function; that's not the question. If you say you have not been involved in any military decisions. Now, yesterday you testified that there was no chain of command. Now, if you have not been involved in any military decisions, how do you know that there was no chain of command?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the free territories around Tuzla and in Tuzla. That's where people remained in their homes, and I'm not comparing that with the occupied territories where ethnic cleansing had been carried out. That's where there was nothing. Everybody could see that among the European and world monitors who toured the area. They, themselves, did not have the freedom to move around freely. The international community and the international --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: My question was with regard to the relationship between different commanders in this area, whether there was a chain of command. And do I recollect -- do I -- is it correct to say that you do not have own knowledge with regard to this relationship?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the territories of those municipalities where I was, let alone in the territories which were enclaves. It was impossible to establish any contacts and it was not within my purview to issue any orders, because there was the military, they had their channels, and they couldn't even use their own channels in some given periods. Nothing was possible there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Now, another point. You testified about attempts to consolidate your resistance in the enclaves, and you testified that Mr. Naser Oric was put forth as the commander of the subregion. Now, what do you mean, this "put forth"? I don't know whether -- what the language in Bosnian/Serbian/Croatian will be, but what do you mean as he was "put forth" as the commander of the subregion?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that attempts were made there to create a body of subregional nature in military and political terms. However, if you look at the dates, if you look at everything that was going on at the time, this body never took off the ground. I said that Mr. Naser Oric was proposed as the commander of the armed forces. Muhamed Salihovic was proposed as the president of the War Presidency of the region. Mr. Hodzic was proposed as the Chief of Staff. However, looking at the time when they met and when you look at the developments in Cerska and Konjevic Polje, you can see that this subregion never took off the ground nor it could take off the ground. If you look everything in -- if you put everything in perspective, the territory and the situation, everything was just a -- on paper.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. Of course there is a difference between whether it took off the ground or whether something was initiated, but at any rate he had been proposed to be commander of the subregion. Now, who proposed him to be commander of the subregion?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really couldn't say. I know that the meeting was held in November; I know that from Mr. Ferid Hodzic, and I don't know all the details. I don't know who the proposal came from. I don't even know who was present. Not only these three people were present there, but I wouldn't want to speculate as to who proposed whom because I am not privy to that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: What if somebody would be proposed to be -- become commander of the subregion, which I think is quite an important position, so there must be certain merits to propose a person to become commander. Do you know what merits played a role here?

utterances.speaker: IZET REDZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there. I wouldn't talk about anybody's merits or strengths or weaknesses. I wasn't there. I did not have the complete information. I don't know what made them propose certain names for certain positions. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ESER
utterances.text: Okay. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you, Judge Eser. And I thank you, Mr. Redzic. I thank you on behalf of the Tribunal, but particularly on behalf of Judge Brydensholt, Judge Eser, and myself for having come over to give testimony in this case. Your testimony is over now. You will be escorted very soon by our usher out of this courtroom, and you will receive all the assistance you require -- wait. I haven't finished. You will receive all the assistance you require to facilitate your return back home at the earliest. But before you leave this courtroom, again on behalf of everyone present here, I should like to wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank the Trial Chamber and all those present in this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Di Fazio, I don't think you can cover what you needed to cover in two minutes. So what I suggest is that you take advantage of how the circumstances developed. And after we leave, you try to have a short tete-a-tete chat with your counterparts. And then tomorrow morning, hopefully, you will be able to announce, both of you together, that a modus vivendi has been reached on these documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or else if you're still not fine-tuned together, you will let me know. We'll hear what the position is and we'll deal with it first thing in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So we are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Tomorrow in the afternoon? Are we meeting in the afternoon tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: We have no witness, though, tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Is the other one not Dachy --

utterances.speaker: MR. JONES
utterances.text: Dachy, he's arriving on Saturday, being proofed over the weekend. We're happy to deal with this Monday morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's fine. I've got no problem. I understand the Defence's problems. One, and, yes, we'll talk, as you have suggested. But there's only one matter that I just want to very, very briefly raise, and that's this, and this is not my submission on the summaries. I want to say more about it. However, the upcoming witnesses, in particular one of them is Mr. Bekric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: And my colleague --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, it's the fourth one.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Mr. Wubben is going to -- is going to take that witness and I'll have Dachy. Now, I don't need to go into the summaries chapter and verse. Suffice it to say, we regard these as nothing more than indications of areas, topics, a list of topics, at least for the relevant parts. I'm not talking about the background material. We propose to resolve this in an amicable way with the Defence. We propose to get more details. We hope that we can, and it's particularly pressing for the upcoming witnesses, particularly pressing. After the break it will be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I told you to try and --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: So, if we can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- keep the bridges that you have built throughout the case between you and intact as possible. The moment you start --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Exactly. I agree, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- destroying them, then we will have big problems in reconstructing them or others.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So this is my exaltation to you. And I am sure that you are not the kind of lawyers that --

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: No. We know we are not entitled to statements and we're not seeking that sort of detail. What we're seeking is what the Rules tell us we're entitled to, a summary of the facts, that's all --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, if it is necessary, let's refine this. We are nonetheless available at all times here. If after we leave now you end up miles apart on these issues and these issues need to be addressed either tomorrow or Friday, please do let us know via the registrar and we will reconvene tomorrow or Friday as necessary. And we will have all the time in the world you require to have this threshed out here and then decided upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: That's an admirable solution, with respect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to be here, so there's no point in forcing issues when they can be discussed -- they can be discussed. But first, try to reach an agreement between you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DI FAZIO
utterances.text: Just one more thing, if I may. I should point out that there have already been some conversations between Mr. Wubben and Madam Vidovic. I don't want that to suddenly -- the fact that I didn't mention that to suddenly be cause for concern on the part of the Defence. I made my submissions knowing that Mr. Wubben had earlier this morning spoken to Madam Vidovic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to speak more. From what I smell in the air, you need to speak more. Let us know. If there is definitely two diametrically opposed positions at the end of the discussions that you will have, please let us know so that we can organise a sitting for tomorrow. That's it. Madam Vidovic, sit down. Finished.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we have agreed on everything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I would expect is the two parties to contact you if they need a sitting tomorrow, in which case you need to advise everyone, in which case you need to advise everyone so that we will have a sitting tomorrow. In other words, let's -- when I said "we are available," we are truly available. And if I were to tell you how much work we have in other cases to deal with, you would be little surprised at all. I mean, the thing is: We need to know, however, if we are sitting or not because certain work can be done here; certain work can be done at home. And we won't be here if we can work at home. At least we can have some fresh air at home which we cannot here. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
